title: Refute the misconception learners bring
statement: When learners bring a common wrong belief, draw it out once at the start as a prediction and refute it, since a clear explanation alone can leave it standing.
example: In one study, refuting the misconception beat a concise correct explanation on immediate gains by an effect size of about 0.79.
detail: A short-video BrainLift in the course plans holds that a clear explanation can produce the feeling of understanding while the misconception survives, and that a video should open by confronting a documented misconception when it is central, citing refutation ≈ d 0.79 and dialogue ≈ d 0.83 over concise correct exposition on immediate conceptual gains (Muller 2008) (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-generation-human-v0.2.md`, lines 113-118). A generic instruction BrainLift sorts misconceptions by source: instinctive ones are taught explicitly with contrastive material and revisited, while ones produced by poor instruction are not foregrounded but designed out of the explanation (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Generic Instruction BrainLift.md`, lines 60-61). The wrong belief is drawn out as a prediction on the same question the lesson answers, and is not voiced again once refuted (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/video-red-team/references/rubric.md`, lines 63-73; `ti-courseplans-audit/skills/course-red-team/SKILL.md`, lines 201-202).
against: The BrainLift scopes the evidence to immediate gains in undergraduates where the misconception is central, not a proven delayed-retention benefit (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-generation-human-v0.2.md`, lines 117-119); and in a study of short narrated videos, refutation text structures largely made no significant difference against an expository one (Schroeder et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331211070534). The study is cited as a dissertation with no DOI or URL in these files, and introductory or overview lessons are exempt and may open on plain curiosity (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/video-red-team/references/rubric.md`).

evidence.quote: When a documented misconception is central, open by confronting it.
A clear explanation can produce the feeling of understanding while the misconception survives.
concise correct exposition on immediate conceptual gains (Muller 2008: refutation ≈ d 0.79, dialogue ≈ d 0.83) [20]. Scope: immediate, undergraduate, misconception-central
teach explicitly with contrastive material; expect to revisit.
don't foreground — fix the explanation so it isn't produced.
A clear explanation that never engages the prior belief produces confident non-learning (Muller: clear-only exposition barely moved scores; misconception-first nearly doubled the gain).
The wrong belief is voiced at most once, at the open, and never rehearsed/scolded in the body
where the teaching atom owns a named misconception, the opener must ELICIT the intuitive wrong belief ONCE (as an invited prediction / reasonable guess), then resolve it against that tension.
They must be the same conceptual question, and the positive body must explicitly resolve the prediction raised at the open.
If deleting the hook leaves the body teaching an unrelated objective unchanged, the hook is misaligned.
Intro/overview atoms are exempt (curiosity hook ok).
thing the learner reads and encodes as the section title, so a negative card **frames the whole lesson via the wrong belief** even when the narration is clean.
**Positive on-screen `[CARD]` labels** — cards must be positive schema labels, never "what X is NOT" / "Not a…"; rewrite negation-phrased catalog cells positively.
Refutation-text research puts the harm in *dwelling on / repeating* the wrong belief, not in *naming it once* to build the boundary.
In the **body** (everything after the hook) **never** narrate the wrong belief ("you might think the sun feeds the plant, but…") — repeating it aloud rehearses it.
A version that first surfaces the intuitive wrong idea, lets the learner feel it is wrong, then resolves it, nearly doubled the gain.
but **never engaged the learner's prior belief** — the exact Muller failure.
